outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the Office of Special Counsel, and the factual and procedural context that gave rise to this litigation. It traces AFL's FOIA request to DOJ, its complaint to OSC, the district court's ruling on the merits, and the appeal to the D.C. Circuit.
subtopics: The Office of Special Counsel: purpose and function within the federal civil service system
AFL's FOIA request to DOJ and its allegations of arbitrary withholding
AFL's complaint to OSC invoking Section 1216
OSC's refusal to investigate based on Section 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates
District court's ruling: legal error by OSC but discretionary authority under Section 1216(c)
OSC's second refusal after remand and final judgment
Appeal and the court's decision to order supplemental briefing on standing

outline.chapter_title: The Statutory Framework Governing OSC's Authority
outline.description: This chapter examines the relevant statutory provisions that define OSC's investigative and enforcement powers, including Section 1216, Section 1214, and FOIA's Section 552(a)(4)(F)(i). Understanding these provisions is essential to comprehending the parties' arguments and the jurisdictional question.
subtopics: OSC's general authority to investigate prohibited personnel practices under the Civil Service Reform Act
Section 1216(a)(3): mandatory investigation of arbitrary FOIA withholdings
Section 1216(c): OSC's authority to seek corrective and disciplinary action for FOIA violations
Section 1214: procedures for corrective actions and notification requirements
Section 552(a)(4)(F)(i): FOIA's separate enforcement provision requiring court order before OSC disciplinary proceedings
The relationship between Section 1216 and Section 552(a)(4)(F)(i): competing interpretations of OSC's authority

outline.chapter_title: Article III Standing Doctrine and Procedural Injury
outline.description: This chapter explains the constitutional requirements for Article III standing and the special doctrines that apply when plaintiffs allege procedural injuries. It provides the legal foundation necessary to understand why the court resolved this case on jurisdictional grounds.
subtopics: Article III's case-or-controversy requirement and its constitutional basis
The three elements of standing: injury in fact, causation, and redressability
Requirements for injury in fact: concrete, particularized, actual or imminent
Procedural injury doctrine: when violation of a procedural right can confer standing
Relaxed standards for imminence and redressability in procedural injury cases
Informational injury: standing based on denial of information to which plaintiff is statutorily entitled
The requirement that procedural rights must be tied to a concrete interest

outline.chapter_title: Application: AFL's Standing Theories and the Court's Analysis
outline.description: This chapter applies standing doctrine to AFL's two asserted theories of injury, examining why both failed to satisfy Article III requirements. It details the court's reasoning on causation, redressability, and the absence of a statutory entitlement to information.
subtopics: AFL's first theory: injury from not receiving FOIA records from DOJ
Causation problems: tracing the injury to DOJ rather than OSC
Redressability problems: the speculative causal chain involving OSC, MSPB, and DOJ
The principle that courts cannot rely on speculation about independent actors not before the court
Heckler v. Chaney and enforcement discretion: courts generally may not compel agency action
AFL's second theory: informational injury from not receiving investigation notices
Why Section 1216 does not create a statutory entitlement to information
The discretionary nature of Section 1214 notice requirements in Section 1216 investigations
Why AFL failed under both ordinary and relaxed standing standards

outline.description: This chapter addresses the court's ultimate disposition, including the vacatur of the district court's judgment and remand for dismissal. It also discusses the broader significance of the case for understanding the limits of judicial power to compel agency enforcement action.
subtopics: The court's holding: AFL lacks Article III standing
Vacatur of the district court's judgment and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
The importance of addressing standing before reaching the merits
Implications for future cases seeking to compel OSC investigations
The separation-of-powers dimension: courts cannot compel agency enforcement decisions
Practical considerations for litigants seeking OSC enforcement of FOIA rights

outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and Judicial Review Standards
outline.description: This chapter explains the procedural posture of the case and the standards governing judicial review at each stage. Understanding the procedural context is essential to appreciating how the standing question arose and why the court resolved it as it did.
subtopics: Motion to dismiss stage: pleading requirements for standing
De novo review standard on appeal
The court's authority to raise standing issues sua sponte
Supplemental briefing ordered by the court
Why the court addressed standing before reaching the merits
The distinction between merits dismissals and jurisdictional dismissals
